A payer must request a refund from their payment service provider within **8 weeks** from the date on which the funds were debited [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 80].

Note that if the payer is not a consumer, micro-enterprise, or charity, the parties may agree that these refund rights do not apply [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 63(5)].

answer:
Generally, a customer cannot revoke a payment order once it has been received by their bank [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 83(1)]. However, there are specific rules for different types of payments:

*   **Direct Debits:** The customer cannot revoke the payment after the end of the business day preceding the day agreed for debiting the funds [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 83(3)].
*   **Future-dated payments:** If a specific day was agreed for execution, the order cannot be revoked after the end of the business day preceding that day [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 83(4)].
*   **PISP or Payee-initiated payments:** The payer cannot revoke the order after giving consent to the payment initiation service provider or the payee [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 83(2)].

After these time limits, a payment order can only be revoked if the customer and the bank agree (and, for payee-initiated transactions, the payee also agrees) [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 83(5)]. The bank may charge for such a revocation if the contract allows it [payment_services_regs_2017, regulation 83(6)].

An electronic money issuer may only charge a fee for redemption if the fee is stated in the contract and one of the following applies:
*   Redemption is requested before the contract is terminated.
*   The holder terminates the contract before the agreed termination date.
*   Redemption is requested more than one year after the contract was terminated.

Any such fee must be "proportionate and commensurate with the costs actually incurred by the electronic money issuer" [electronic_money_regs_2011, regulation 41]. Additionally, the contract must clearly and prominently state these conditions and fees before the holder is bound by it [electronic_money_regs_2011, regulation 40].

The Treasury is responsible for making arrangements for the national proliferation financing risk assessment and preparing a report on its findings [money_laundering_regs_2017, regulation 16A(1)-(4)].

Regarding its own proliferation financing controls, a firm must:
* Take appropriate steps (taking into account its size and nature) to identify and assess its proliferation financing risks, using the Treasury's report and specific risk factors (such as customers, countries, products, transactions, and delivery channels), keep a written record of these steps, and provide them to its supervisory authority on request [money_laundering_regs_2017, regulation 18A].
* Establish, maintain, regularly review, and update proportionate policies, controls, and procedures—approved by senior management—to effectively mitigate and manage those risks, including risk management practices, internal controls, monitoring, and specific measures for complex transactions, anonymity risks, and new products or technologies [money_laundering_regs_2017, regulation 19A(1)-(4)].
* Maintain written records of these policies, controls, procedures, changes, and internal communications, and communicate them to relevant foreign branches and subsidiaries [money_laundering_regs_2017, regulation 19A(1), (5)].

Payment Services Regulations 2017, regulation 106A(1)-(4) - Technical standards
1 The FCA may make technical standards specifying— a requirements that must be met by the strong customer authentication referred to in regulation 100(1) and (2); b exemptions from the application of regulation 100(1), (2) and (3), based on the criteria specified in paragraph (3) of this regulation; c the requirements with which security measures have to comply, in accordance with regulation 100(3), in order to protect the confidentiality and integrity of the payment service users' personalised security credentials; d the requirements for common and secure open standards of communication for the purpose of identification, authentication, notification and information, as well as for the implementation of security measures, between account servicing payment service providers, payment initiation service providers, account information service providers, payers, payees and other payment service providers. 2 In making technical standards under this regulation, the FCA must have regard to the need to— a ensure an appropriate level of security for payment service users and payment service providers through the adoption of effective and risk-based requirements; b ensure the safety of payment service users' funds and personal data; c secure and maintain fair competition among all payment service providers; d ensure technology and business-model neutrality; e allow for the development of user-friendly, accessible and innovative means of payment. 3 The exemptions referred to in paragraph (1)(b) must be based on— a the level of risk involved in the service provided; b the amount of the transaction, its recurrence, or both; c the payment channel used for the execution of the transaction. 4 The FCA must review and, if appropriate, update the technical standards on a regular basis in order (among other things) to take account of innovation and technological developments.

[money_laundering_regs_2017, regulation 30ZA(5)]
Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations 2017, regulation 30ZA(5) - Insolvent bank customers
5 In this regulation— “ insolvency date ” in respect of an insolvent bank means the date on which a bank insolvency order is made in relation to the bank under section 94 (the order) of the Banking Act 2009. “ insolvent bank ” means either— a bank as defined in section 2 (interpretation: “bank”) of the Banking Act 2009 that has entered into the procedure in Part 2 of that Act; or a building society as defined in section 119 (interpretation) of the Building Societies Act 1986 that has entered into the procedure in Part 2 of the Banking Act 2009, as applied and modified by section 90C (application of bank insolvency and administration legislation to building societies) of the Building Societies Act 1986; “ insolvent bank customer ” means any customer— which the credit institution is reasonably satisfied was a customer of an insolvent bank at the insolvency date in respect of that insolvent bank; and with whom the credit institution begins to establish a business relationship within the period of 30 days beginning with the insolvency date in respect of that insolvent bank.
